attribution.note: Section heading in Zitron's own post. He wrote and endorses it.

semantics.note: The normalised proposition matches the heading. Causal kind fits: it explains why ROI can't be measured by saying no ROI exists. The heading is categorical and somewhat rhetorical, but the wording is firm.

contract.note: Reading it as generative AI and net positive organisational return, with full costs counted, is an ordinary plain reading. One credible full-cost counterexample is a fair test of a universal claim. The cost boundary is the evaluator's, not the speaker's.

evidence.note: Deloitte survey published 2025-10-22. An anonymous executive reports positive returns, but there is no deployment-level cost accounting and the initiative isn't clearly generative AI. This doesn't meet the contradiction bar.
Preprint v4, available 2026-06-01. It shows measured sales gains, but the authors say they can't estimate full ROI. It doesn't establish net ROI either way.

reviews.rationale: Neither item gives a full-cost, attributable, positive net ROI for a deployment, so the claim isn't contradicted. Nothing shows a universal absence of returns, or that such an absence causes the measurement difficulty, so it isn't supported either. The packet doesn't settle the claim.

attribution.note: Zitron's own sentence in his post.

semantics.note: Faithful, and 'at best' is kept as a lower bound. It's a general assertion about facility economics. For modern AI facilities it is partly projective, since few have five years of service, but observation is an acceptable kind.

contract.note: Separating periodic loss from capital recovery is a fair, ordinary reading. The Q1 2026 reference period chosen by the evaluator can't test a multi-year loss duration. The contract admits this and asks for facility histories, which no source here provides.

evidence.note: Epoch's stylised cost model (2026-05-14) supports the scale of upfront capex ($38B per GW). It gives no realised revenue or profit history, so it can't test the loss duration.
CoreWeave's Q1 2026 company disclosure gives consolidated results, not facility-level profit histories over first service years.

reviews.rationale: Multibillion upfront costs are plausible from the cost model. The core claim, at least five or six years of losses per facility, needs facility-level operating histories, and the packet has none. Consolidated operator results and modelled costs don't settle it either way.

attribution.note: Zitron's own sentence in his post.

semantics.note: 'Won't do it' is firm language, and 'do it' means make AI cheaper. In context, 'AI' means the cost of running and training LLMs, which the proposition leaves implicit. No horizon is given.

contract.note: The early-resolution rule lets one cheaper workload on a named chip refute the claim. That includes non-LLM tasks, such as a vision model. Zitron's point is about the aggregate cost of generative AI/LLM services not falling. Reading it as 'any single workload saving' stretches it against him.

evidence.note: AWS/Tomofun company disclosure: an 83% cost cut on Inferentia2 for a vision model. Published 2026-05-06, before the forecast. Not a post-publication outcome, and not LLM-scale.
DeepSeek's own preprint (2026-09-17) claims lower deployment costs. It's a self-claim with no matched realised cost comparison.
Independent preprint (2026-10-25): one training workload ran 25% cheaper per run on TPU. It's a single research experiment with high migration failure and human costs, not deployed AI service cost.

reviews.rationale: The forecast has no deadline, and no dated post-publication event in the packet conclusively shows a named technology lowering the comparable cost of generative AI work. The items are pre-publication, self-reported, or single training experiments. The contract's single-deployment refutation standard is also broader than the speaker's meaning.

attribution.note: Zitron's own sentence in his post.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps the deployment premise, the claim that nobody says profitable or sustainable, and the causal attribution to NVIDIA's priorities. The motive attribution is partly rhetorical.

contract.note: Scoping 'nobody' to principal launch communications, and requiring causal evidence for the motive, is fair. Treating efficiency marketing as proof of neither profitability nor motive is also reasonable.

evidence.note: CoreWeave company disclosure (2026-06-01) confirms the first cloud bring-up of Vera Rubin NVL72, with Dell systems. That supports the deployment premise only, and only as the first cloud bring-up. It also makes efficiency and cost-per-token claims.
Dell company disclosure (2026-06-01) stresses efficiency and lower cost per token. The excerpt doesn't call the systems profitable or sustainable, and it says nothing about NVIDIA's motive.

reviews.rationale: The bring-up premise is supported by contemporaneous company records, as the first cloud bring-up. The launch excerpts don't use 'profitable' or 'sustainable,' but the core causal claim about NVIDIA's priorities has no evidence for or against it. Efficiency marketing neither proves nor disproves the motive.
